content: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection that can occur in any part of the urinary system, including the bladder, kidneys, ureters, or urethra. The specific name of the infection depends on the location within the urinary tract. An infection in the bladder is referred to as cystitis or a bladder infection. An infection in one or both kidneys is called pyelonephritis or a kidney infection. Infections in the ureters, the tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder, are rare. An infection in the urethra, the tube that expels urine from the bladder to the outside, is called urethritis. Symptoms of a UTI Symptoms of a bladder infection may include: Cloudy or bloody urine, often accompanied by a foul or strong odor. A low-grade fever, though not everyone with a UTI will develop a fever. Pain or a burning sensation during urination. Pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen (typically in the middle) or back. A persistent and strong urge to urinate frequently, even after the bladder has been emptied. If the infection spreads to the kidneys, additional symptoms may include: Chills, shaking, or night sweats. Fatigue and a general feeling of being unwell. A fever exceeding 101°F. Pain in the flank (side), back, or groin. Flushed, warm, or reddened skin. Mental changes or confusion, particularly in elderly individuals, where these may be the only signs of a UTI. Nausea and vomiting. Severe abdominal pain in some cases. Causes of UTIs UTIs are typically caused by bacteria that enter the urethra and travel to the bladder. In most cases, the body can eliminate these bacteria. However, women are more prone to UTIs due to their shorter urethra and its proximity to the anus. Certain factors increase the likelihood of developing a UTI, including: Sexual activity, particularly in women, as germs can be introduced into the urethra. Use of diaphragms for birth control. Menopause, which alters the urinary tract environment. Diabetes. Advanced age, especially in individuals residing in nursing homes. Incomplete bladder emptying (urinary retention). Use of urinary catheters, which can introduce bacteria into the urinary tract. Bowel incontinence. Conditions that obstruct urine flow, such as an enlarged prostate, narrowed urethra, or kidney stones. Prolonged immobility, such as during recovery from a hip fracture. Pregnancy. Recent surgery or procedures involving the urinary tract. High-Risk Groups Women are at higher risk for UTIs due to anatomical factors and activities such as sexual intercourse, bowel movements, or the use of certain birth control methods like diaphragms. Individuals with urinary catheters or weakened immune systems are also at increased risk. Diagnosis To diagnose a UTI, a urine sample is typically collected for testing. Urinalysis is performed to detect white blood cells, red blood cells, bacteria, and specific chemicals like nitrites in the urine. This test is often sufficient for diagnosis. Urine culture may be conducted to identify the specific bacteria causing the infection and ensure the correct antibiotic is prescribed. In some cases, a complete blood count (CBC) and blood culture may be performed. Additional tests may be recommended to identify underlying urinary system issues that could contribute to recurrent or difficult-to-treat infections. These tests include: CT scan of the abdomen. Intravenous pyelogram (IVP). Kidney scan. Kidney ultrasound. Voiding cystourethrogram. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your healthcare provider if you experience symptoms of a UTI. Seek immediate medical attention if you develop: Back or side pain. Chills. Fever. Vomiting. These symptoms may indicate a kidney infection. Additionally, consult your provider if you have been treated for a UTI but symptoms return shortly after completing antibiotics. Treatment Options Treatment depends on the severity of the infection. Mild Bladder and Kidney Infections Oral antibiotics are typically prescribed to prevent the infection from spreading to the kidneys. For a simple bladder infection, women usually take antibiotics for 3 days, while men may require 7–14 days. For bladder infections with complications (e.g., pregnancy or diabetes) or mild kidney infections, antibiotics are usually taken for 7–14 days. It is crucial to complete the full course of antibiotics, even if symptoms improve, to prevent recurrence or antibiotic resistance. Commonly prescribed antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, Augmentin, doxycycline, and fluoroquinolones. Your doctor may also prescribe medications like phenazopyridine hydrochloride (Pyridium) to relieve burning pain and the urgent need to urinate, but antibiotics are still necessary. Drinking plenty of fluids is recommended for all individuals with bladder or kidney infections. For women with recurrent bladder infections, preventive strategies may include: Taking a single dose of antibiotics after sexual activity to prevent post-coital infections. Keeping a 3-day course of antibiotics at home for self-treatment based on symptoms. Taking a single daily dose of antibiotics to prevent recurrent infections. Severe Kidney Infections Hospitalization may be required if you are severely ill, unable to take oral medications, or unable to stay hydrated. Hospitalization may also be necessary for individuals who are elderly, have kidney stones or anatomical abnormalities, have recently undergone urinary tract surgery, or have underlying medical conditions such as cancer, diabetes, multiple sclerosis, or spinal cord injuries. Pregnant individuals with fever or other signs of illness may also require hospitalization. In the hospital, treatment typically involves intravenous fluids and antibiotics. Chronic UTIs Some individuals experience recurrent or persistent UTIs that do not resolve with standard treatment. These are referred to as chronic UTIs. Chronic UTIs may require long-term antibiotic therapy or stronger antibiotics. If a structural abnormality in the urinary tract is identified as the cause, surgery may be recommended. Prognosis While UTIs can be uncomfortable, treatment is usually effective. Symptoms of a bladder infection typically resolve within 24–48 hours after starting treatment. Kidney infections may take a week or longer for symptoms to subside.
